Overview of the ML-KEM Scheme\nThis section gives a high-level overview of the ML-KEM scheme.\n\n3.1 Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms\nThe following is a high-level overview of key-encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs). For details, see\nSP 800-227 [1].\nA KEM is a cryptographic scheme that, under certain conditions, can be used to establish a shared\nsecret key between two communicating parties. This shared secret key can then be used for\nsymmetric-key cryptography.\nA KEM consists of three algorithms and a collection of parameter sets. The three algorithms are:\n     1. A probabilistic key generation algorithm denoted by KeyGen\n     2. A probabilistic ”encapsulation” algorithm denoted by Encaps\n     3. A deterministic ”decapsulation” algorithm denoted by Decaps\nThe collection of parameter sets is used to select a trade-off between security and efficiency.\nEach parameter set in the collection is a list of specific (typically numerical) values, one for each\nparameter required by the three algorithms.\n\n                     Alice                                              Bob\n\n                    KeyGen\n\n\n\n\n                decapsulation key                                 encapsulation key\n\n\n\n\n                    Decaps                  ciphertext                Encaps\n\n\n\n                Alice’s copy of the                               Bob’s copy of the\n                shared secret key                                 shared secret key\n\n                       𝐾′                                                𝐾\n                   Figure 1. A simple view of key establishment using a KEM\n\n\n                                                12\n\n\nFIPS 203                                       MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\nIn the typical application, a KEM is used to establish a shared secret key between two parties\n(here referred to as Alice and Bob) as described in Figure 1. Alice begins by running KeyGen in\norder to generate a (public) encapsulation key and a (private) decapsulation key. Upon obtaining\nAlice’s encapsulation key, Bob runs the Encaps algorithm, which produces Bob’s copy 𝐾 of the\nshared secret key along with an associated ciphertext. Bob sends the ciphertext to Alice, and\nAlice completes the process by running the Decaps algorithm using her decapsulation key and\nthe ciphertext. This final step produces Alice’s copy 𝐾 ′ of the shared secret key.\nAfter completing this process, Alice and Bob would like to conclude that their outputs satisfy\n𝐾 ′ = 𝐾 and that this value is a secure, random, shared secret key. However, these properties\nonly hold if certain important conditions are satisfied, as discussed in SP 800-227 [1].\n\n3.2 The ML-KEM Scheme\nML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism based on CRYSTALS-KYBER [4], a scheme that was\ninitially described in [8]. The following is a brief and informal description of the computational\nassumption underlying ML-KEM and how the ML-KEM scheme is constructed.\n\nThe computational assumption. The security of ML-KEM is based on the presumed hardness\nof the so-called Module Learning with Errors (MLWE) problem [9], which is a generalization of\nthe Learning With Errors (LWE) problem introduced by Regev in 2005 [10]. The hardness of the\nMLWE problem is itself based on the presumed hardness of certain computational problems in\nmodule lattices [9]. This motivates the name of the scheme ML-KEM.\nIn the LWE problem, the input is a set of random “noisy” linear equations in some secret\nvariables 𝑥 ∈ ℤ𝑛𝑞 , and the task is to recover 𝑥. The noise in the equations is such that standard\nalgorithms (e.g., Gaussian elimination) are intractable. The LWE problem naturally lends itself to\ncryptographic applications. For example, if 𝑥 is interpreted as a secret key, then one can encrypt\na one-bit plaintext value by sampling either an approximately correct linear equation (if the\nplaintext is zero) or a far-from-correct linear equation (if the plaintext is one). Plausibly, only a\nparty in possession of 𝑥 can distinguish these two cases. Encryption can then be delegated to\nanother party by publishing a large collection of noisy linear equations, which can be combined\nappropriately by the encrypting party. The result is an asymmetric encryption scheme.\nThe MLWE problem is similar to the LWE problem. An important difference is that, in MLWE, ℤ𝑛𝑞\nis replaced by a certain module 𝑅𝑞𝑘 , which is constructed by taking the 𝑘-fold Cartesian product\nof a certain polynomial ring 𝑅𝑞 . In particular, the secret in the MLWE problem is an element 𝐱 of\nthe module 𝑅𝑞𝑘 . The ring 𝑅𝑞 is discussed in detail in Section 4.3.\n\nThe ML-KEM construction. At a high level, the construction of the scheme ML-KEM proceeds in\ntwo steps. First, the ideas discussed previously are used to construct a public-key encryption (PKE)\nscheme from the MLWE problem. Second, this PKE scheme is converted into a key-encapsulation\nmechanism using the so-called Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transform [11, 12]. Due to certain prop-\nerties of the FO transform, the resulting KEM provides security in a significantly more general\nattack model than the PKE scheme. As a result, ML-KEM is believed to satisfy so-called IND-CCA2\nsecurity [1, 4, 13, 14].\n\n                                                 13\n\n\nFIPS 203                                       MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\nThe specification of the ML-KEM algorithms in this standard will follow the same pattern. Specif-\nically, this standard will first describe a public-key encryption scheme called K-PKE (in Section 5)\nand then use the algorithms of K-PKE as subroutines when describing the algorithms of ML-KEM\n(in Sections 6 and 7). The cryptographic transformation from K-PKE to ML-KEM is crucial for\nachieving IND-CCA2 security. The scheme K-PKE is not IND-CCA2-secure and shall not be used as\na stand-alone scheme (see Section 3.3).\nA notable feature of ML-KEM is the use of the number-theoretic transform (NTT). The NTT\n                                                                            ̂ linear polynomials.\nconverts a polynomial 𝑓 ∈ 𝑅𝑞 to an alternative representation as a vector 𝑓 of\nWorking with NTT representations enables significantly faster multiplication of polynomials.\nOther operations (e.g., addition, rounding, and sampling) can be done in either representation.\nML-KEM satisfies the essential KEM property of correctness. This means that in the absence\nof corruption or interference, the process in Figure 1 will result in 𝐾 ′ = 𝐾 with overwhelming\nprobability. ML-KEM also comes with a proof of asymptotic theoretical security in a certain\nheuristic model [4]. Each of the parameter sets of ML-KEM comes with an associated security\nstrength that was estimated based on current cryptanalysis (see Section 8 for details).\n\nParameter sets and algorithms. Recall that a KEM consists of algorithms KeyGen, Encaps, and\nDecaps, along with a collection of parameter sets. In the case of ML-KEM, the three aforemen-\ntioned algorithms are:\n   1. ML-KEM.KeyGen (Algorithm 19)\n   2. ML-KEM.Encaps (Algorithm 20)\n   3. ML-KEM.Decaps (Algorithm 21)\nThese algorithms are described and discussed in detail in Section 7.\nML-KEM comes equipped with three parameter sets:\n    • ML-KEM-512 (security category 1)\n    • ML-KEM-768 (security category 3)\n    • ML-KEM-1024 (security category 5)\nThese parameter sets are described and discussed in detail in Section 8. The security categories\n1-5 are defined in SP 800-57, Part 1 [7]. Each parameter set assigns a particular numerical value\nto five integer variables: 𝑘, 𝜂1 , 𝜂2 , 𝑑𝑢 , and 𝑑𝑣 . The values of these variables in each parameter\nset are given in Table 2 of Section 8. In addition to these five variable parameters, there are also\ntwo constants: 𝑛 = 256 and 𝑞 = 3329.\n\nDecapsulation failures. Provided that all inputs are well-formed and randomness generation is\nsuccessful, the key establishment procedure of ML-KEM will never explicitly fail, meaning that\nboth ML-KEM.Encaps and ML-KEM.Decaps will each output a 256-bit value. Moreover, if no\ncorruption or interference is present, the two 256-bit values produced by ML-KEM.Encaps and\nML-KEM.Decaps will be equal with overwhelming probability (i.e., 𝐾 ′ will equal 𝐾 in the process\ndescribed in Figure 1). The event that 𝐾 ′ ≠ 𝐾 under these conditions is called a decapsulation\n\n                                                 14\n\n\nFIPS 203                                       MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\nfailure. Formally, the decapsulation failure probability is defined to be the probability (conditioned\non no RGB failures) that the process\n\n                                 1. (ek, dk) ← ML-KEM.KeyGen()                                   (3.1)\n                                 2. (𝑐, 𝐾) ← ML-KEM.Encaps(ek)                                   (3.2)\n                                 3. 𝐾 ′ ← ML-KEM.Decaps(dk, 𝑐)                                   (3.3)\n\nresults in 𝐾 ′ ≠ 𝐾. The probability is taken over uniformly random seeds 𝑑, 𝑧 (sampled in\nML-KEM.KeyGen) and 𝑚 (sampled in ML-KEM.Encaps) and under the heuristic assumption that\nhash functions and XOFs behave like uniformly random functions. The decapsulation failure rates\nfor ML-KEM are listed in Table 1. For details, see Theorem 1 in [8] and the scripts in [15].\n\n                        Table 1. Decapsulation failure rates for ML-KEM\n\n                           Parameter set     Decapsulation failure rate\n                           ML-KEM-512                2−138.8\n                           ML-KEM-768                2−164.8\n                           ML-KEM-1024               2−174.8\n\n\nTerminology for keys. A KEM involves three different types of keys: encapsulation keys, de-\ncapsulation keys, and shared secret keys. ML-KEM is built on top of the component public-key\nencryption scheme K-PKE, which has two additional key types: encryption keys and decryption\nkeys. In the literature, encapsulation keys and encryption keys are sometimes referred to as\n“public keys,” while decapsulation keys and decryption keys are sometimes referred to as “pri-\nvate keys.” In order to reduce confusion, this standard will not use the terms “public key” or\n“private key.” Instead, keys will be referred to only using the more specific terms, i.e., one of\n“encapsulation key”, “decapsulation key”, “encryption key”, “decryption key”, and “shared secret\nkey”.\n\n3.3 Requirements for ML-KEM Implementations\nThis section describes several requirements for cryptographic modules that implement ML-KEM.\nImplementation requirements specific to particular algorithms will be described in later sections.\nAdditional requirements, including requirements for using ML-KEM in specific applications,\nare given in SP 800-227 [1]. While conforming implementations must adhere to all of these\nrequirements, adherence does not guarantee that the result will be secure (see Point 13 in the\nannouncement).\n\nK-PKE is only a component. The public-key encryption scheme K-PKE described in Section 5 shall\nnot be used as a stand-alone cryptographic scheme. Instead, the algorithms that comprise K-PKE\nmay only be used as subroutines in the algorithms of ML-KEM. In particular, the algorithms\nK-PKE.KeyGen (Algorithm 13), K-PKE.Encrypt (Algorithm 14), and K-PKE.Decrypt (Algorithm 15)\nare not approved for use as a public-key encryption scheme.\n\n                                                 15\n\n\nFIPS 203                                     MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\n\n\nControlled access to internal functions. The key-encapsulation mechanism ML-KEM makes use\nof internal, “derandomized” functions ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal, ML-KEM.Encaps_internal, and\nML-KEM.Decaps_internal, specified in Section 6. The interfaces for these functions should not\nbe made available to applications other than for testing purposes. In particular, the sampling of\nrandom values required for key generation (as specified in ML-KEM.KeyGen) and encapsulation\n(as specified in ML-KEM.Encaps) shall be performed by the cryptographic module.\n\nEquivalent implementations. For every algorithm that is specified in this standard, a conforming\nimplementation may replace the given set of steps with any mathematically equivalent set of\nsteps. In other words, the specified algorithm may be replaced with a different procedure that\nproduces the correct output for every input (where “input” includes the specified input as well\nas all parameter values and all randomness).\n\nApproved usage of the shared secret key. If randomness generation is successful, the values\n𝐾 and 𝐾 ′ returned by ML-KEM.Encaps and ML-KEM.Decaps, respectively, are always 256-bit\nvalues. Under appropriate conditions (see Sections 3.1 and 3.2, and SP 800-227 [1]), these values\nmatch (i.e., 𝐾 ′ = 𝐾) and can be used directly as a shared secret key for symmetric cryptography.\nIf further key derivation is needed, the final symmetric keys shall be derived from this 256-bit\nshared secret key in an approved manner, as specified in SP 800-108 and SP 800-56C [16, 17].\nAs discussed in Section 3.2, ML-KEM is an IND-CCA2-secure KEM. However, a combined KEM\nthat includes ML-KEM as a component might not meet IND-CCA2 security. Implementers should\nassess the security of any procedure in which the key derivation methods of SP 800-56C are\napplied to ML-KEM in combination with another key establishment procedure. More guidance\nregarding combined KEMs is given in SP 800-227 [1].\n\nRandomness generation. Two algorithms in this standard require the generation of randomness\nas an internal step: ML-KEM.KeyGen and ML-KEM.Encaps. In pseudocode, this randomness\n                                                          $\ngeneration is denoted by a statement of the form 𝑚 ←− 𝔹32 . A fresh string of random bytes\nmust be generated for every such invocation. These random bytes shall be generated using an\napproved RBG, as prescribed in SP 800-90A, SP 800-90B, and SP 800-90C [18, 19, 20]. Moreover,\nthis RBG shall have a security strength of at least 128 bits for ML-KEM-512, at least 192 bits for\nML-KEM-768, and at least 256 bits for ML-KEM-1024.\n\nInput checking. The algorithms ML-KEM.Encaps and ML-KEM.Decaps require input checking.\nImplementers shall ensure that ML-KEM.Encaps and ML-KEM.Decaps are only executed on\ninputs that have been checked, as described in Section 7.\n\nDestruction of intermediate values. Data used in intermediate computation steps of KEM\nalgorithms could be used by an adversary to compromise security. Therefore, implementers\nshall ensure that intermediate data is destroyed as soon as it is no longer needed. In particular,\nfor ML-KEM.KeyGen, ML-KEM.Encaps, and ML-KEM.Decaps, only the designated output can be\nretained in memory after the algorithm terminates. All other data shall be destroyed prior to\n                                               16\n\n\nFIPS 203                                    MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\nthe algorithm terminating.\nThere are two exceptions to this rule:\n   1. The seed (𝑑, 𝑧) generated in steps 1 and 2 of ML-KEM.KeyGen can be stored for later\n      expansion using ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal. As this seed can be used to compute the\n      decapsulation key, it is sensitive data and shall be treated with the same safeguards as a\n      decapsulation key (see SP 800-227 [1]).\n   2. The matrix 𝐀̂ generated in steps 3-7 of K-PKE.KeyGen (as a subroutine of ML-KEM.KeyGen)\n      can be stored so that it need not be recomputed in later operations (e.g., ML-KEM.Decaps).\n      The same matrix 𝐀̂ is also generated in steps 4-8 of K-PKE.Encrypt (as a subroutine of\n      ML-KEM.Encaps or ML-KEM.Decaps); it can also then be stored. In either case, the matrix\n      𝐀̂ is data that is easily computed from the public encapsulation key and thus does not\n      require any special protections.\n\nNo floating-point arithmetic. Implementations of ML-KEM shall not use floating-point arithmetic,\nas rounding errors in floating-point operations may lead to incorrect results in some cases. In\nall pseudocode in this standard in which division is performed (e.g., 𝑥/𝑦) and 𝑦 may not divide\n𝑥, either ⌊𝑥/𝑦⌋, ⌈𝑥/𝑦⌉, or ⌈𝑥/𝑦⌋ is used. All of these can be computed without floating-point\narithmetic, as ordinary integer division 𝑥/𝑦 computes ⌊𝑥/𝑦⌋, and ⌈𝑥/𝑦⌉ = ⌊(𝑥 + 𝑦 − 1)/𝑦⌋ for\nnon-negative integers 𝑥 and positive integers 𝑦.\n\n\n\n\n                                              17\n\n\nFIPS 203                                      MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\n\n4.     Auxiliary Algorithms\n4.1 Cryptographic Functions\nThe algorithms specified in this publication require the use of several cryptographic functions.\nEach function shall be instantiated by means of an approved hash function or an approved\neXtendable-Output Function (XOF), as prescribed below. The relevant hash functions and XOFs\nare described in detail in FIPS 202 [6]. They will be used as follows.\nSHA3-256 and SHA3-512 are hash functions with one variable-length input and one fixed-length\noutput. In this standard, invocations of these functions on an input 𝑀 will be denoted by\nSHA3-256(𝑀 ) and SHA3-512(𝑀 ), respectively. Importantly, these\nwrappers will avoid any potential “byte array” versus “bit-length” confusion by only working with\nbytes and byte array lengths.\n\nPseudorandom function (PRF). The algorithm ByteEncode\nconverts an array of 𝑛 = 256 integers modulo 𝑚 into a corresponding array of bytes. ByteDecode\nperforms the inverse operation, converting an array of bytes into an array of integers modulo 𝑚.\nSpecifying the modulus 𝑚 is done as described below.\nFor the following description, it is convenient to view ByteDecode and ByteEncode as converting\nbetween integers and bits. The operations are performed in two different ways,\ndepending on the value of 𝑑:\n   • For 𝑑 satisfying 1 ≤ 𝑑 ≤ 11, the conversion is one-to-one. ByteDecode𝑑 converts each\n     𝑑-bit segment of its input into one integer modulo 2𝑑 , while ByteEncode𝑑 performs the\n     inverse operation.\n   • For 𝑑 = 12, ByteDecode12 produces integers modulo 𝑞 as output, while ByteEncode12\n     receives integers modulo 𝑞 as input. Indeed, some 12-bit segments could\n     correspond to an integer greater than 𝑞 − 1 = 3328 but less than 4096. However, this\n     cannot occur for arrays produced by ByteEncode12 . In the case of ML-KEM, the NTT is used to improve the efficiency of\nmultiplication in the ring 𝑅𝑞 . Recall that 𝑅𝑞 is the ring ℤ𝑞 [𝑋]/(𝑋 𝑛 + 1) of polynomials of the\nform 𝑓 = 𝑓0 + 𝑓1 𝑋 + ⋯ + 𝑓255 𝑋 255 (where 𝑓𝑗 ∈ ℤ𝑞 for all 𝑗), with the ring operations defined\nby arithmetic modulo 𝑋 𝑛 + 1.\nThe ring 𝑅𝑞 is isomorphic to another ring 𝑇𝑞 , which is a direct sum of 128 quadratic extensions\nof ℤ𝑞 . The NTT is a computationally efficient isomorphism between these two rings. When a\npolynomial 𝑓 ∈ 𝑅𝑞 is input, the NTT outputs an element 𝑓 ̂ ∶= NTT(𝑓) of the ring 𝑇𝑞 , where 𝑓 is\n                                                                                               ̂\ncalled the “NTT representation” of 𝑓. The isomorphism property implies that\n\n                                  𝑓 ×𝑅𝑞 𝑔 = NTT−1 (𝑓 ×\n                                                     ̂\n                                                       𝑇𝑞 𝑔),\n                                                           ̂                                  (4.9)\n\nwhere ×𝑅𝑞 and ×𝑇𝑞 denote multiplication in 𝑅𝑞 and 𝑇𝑞 , respectively. Moreover, since 𝑇𝑞 is a\nproduct of 128 rings that each consist of polynomials of degree at most one, the operation ×𝑇𝑞\nis much more efficient than the operation ×𝑅𝑞 . For these reasons, the NTT is considered to be\nan integral part of ML-KEM and not merely an optimization.\nAs the rings 𝑅𝑞 and 𝑇𝑞 have a vector space structure over ℤ𝑞 , the most natural abstract data\ntype to represent elements from either of these rings is ℤ𝑛𝑞 . For this reason, the choice of data\nstructure for the inputs and outputs of NTT and NTT−1 are length-𝑛 arrays of integers modulo\n𝑞. These arrays are understood to represent elements of 𝑇𝑞 or 𝑅𝑞 , respectively (see Section\n2.4.4). Algorithms 9 and 10 describe an efficient means of computing NTT and NTT−1 in place.\nHowever, to clarify the distinction between the algebraic objects before and after the conversion,\nthe algorithms are written with explicit inputs and outputs. This is consistent with this standard’s\nconvention that all inputs are passed by copy.\n\nThe mathematical structure of the NTT. In ML-KEM, 𝑞 is the prime 3329 = 28 ⋅ 13 + 1, and\n𝑛 = 256. There are 128 primitive 256-th roots of unity and no primitive 512-th roots of unity in\nℤ𝑞 . Note that 𝜁 = 17 ∈ ℤ𝑞 is a primitive 256-th root of unity modulo 𝑞. Thus, 𝜁 128 ≡ −1.\nDefine BitRev7 (𝑖) to be the integer represented by bit-reversing the unsigned 7-bit value that\ncorresponds to the input integer 𝑖 ∈ {0, … , 127}.\nThe polynomial 𝑋 256 + 1 factors into 128 polynomials of degree 2 modulo 𝑞 as follows:\n\n                                           127\n                              𝑋 256 + 1 = ∏ (𝑋 2 − 𝜁 2BitRev7 (𝑖)+1 ) . The K-PKE Component Scheme\nThis section describes the component scheme K-PKE. As discussed in Section 3.3, K-PKE is not\napproved for use in a stand-alone fashion. It serves only as a collection of subroutines for use in\nthe algorithms of the approved scheme ML-KEM, as described in Section 7.\nK-PKE consists of three algorithms:\n     1. Key generation (K-PKE.KeyGen)\n     2. Encryption (K-PKE.Encrypt)\n     3. Decryption (K-PKE.Decrypt)\nWhen K-PKE is instantiated as part of ML-KEM, K-PKE inherits the parameter set selected for\nML-KEM. Each parameter set specifies numerical values for each parameter. While 𝑛 is always\n256 and 𝑞 is always 3329, the values of the remaining parameters 𝑘, 𝜂1 , 𝜂2 , 𝑑𝑢 , and 𝑑𝑣 vary\namong the three parameter sets. Parameters and parameter sets are described in Section 8.\nThe algorithms in this section do not perform any input checking because they are only invoked as\nsubroutines of the main ML-KEM algorithms. The algorithms of ML-KEM themselves do perform\ninput checking as needed.\nEach of the algorithms of K-PKE is accompanied by a brief, informal description in text. For\nsimplicity, this description is written in terms of vectors and matrices whose entries are elements\nof 𝑅𝑞 . In the actual algorithm, most of the computations occur in the NTT domain in order to\nimprove the efficiency of multiplication. The relevant vectors and matrices will then have entries\nin 𝑇𝑞 . Linear-algebraic arithmetic with such vectors and matrices (e.g., line 18 of K-PKE.KeyGen)\nis performed as described in Sections 2.4.7 and 4.3.1. The encryption and decryption keys of\nK-PKE are also stored in the NTT form.\n\n5.1 K-PKE Key Generation\nThe key generation algorithm K-PKE.KeyGen of K-PKE (Algorithm 13) receives a seed as input and\noutputs an encryption key ekPKE and a decryption key dkPKE . As is typically the case for public-key\nencryption, the encryption key can be made public, while the decryption key and the randomness\nmust remain private. Indeed, the encryption key of K-PKE will serve as the encapsulation key of\nML-KEM (see ML-KEM.KeyGen below) and can thus be made public. Meanwhile, the decryption\nkey and seed of K-PKE.KeyGen must remain private as they can be used to perform decapsulation\nin ML-KEM.\nThe matrix 𝐀̂ generated in steps 3-7 of K-PKE.KeyGen can be stored, as specified in Section 3.3.\nThis allows later operations to use 𝐀̂ directly rather than re-expanding it from the public seed 𝜌.\n\nInformal description. The rows of the\nmatrix 𝐀 form the equation coefficients. This matrix is generated pseudorandomly using XOF\nwith only a seed stored in the encryption key. The algorithm K-PKE.Encrypt begins by extracting the vector 𝐭 and the\nseed from the encryption key. The seed is then expanded to re-generate the matrix 𝐀 in the same\nmanner as was done in K-PKE.KeyGen. If 𝐭 and 𝐀 are derived correctly from an encryption key\nproduced by K-PKE.KeyGen, then they are equal to their corresponding values in K-PKE.KeyGen.\nRecall from the description of key generation that the pair (𝐀, 𝐭 = 𝐀𝐬 + 𝐞) can be thought of as\na system of noisy linear equations in the secret variables 𝐬. One can generate an additional noisy\nlinear equation in the same secret variables — without knowing 𝐬 — by picking a random linear\n\n                                                 30\n\n\nFIPS 203                                      MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\ncombination of the noisy equations in the system (𝐀, 𝐭). One can then encode information in the\n“constant term” (i.e., the entry that is a linear combination of entries of 𝐭) of such a combined\nequation. This information can then be deciphered by a party in possession of 𝐬. For example,\none could encode a single bit by deciding whether or not to significantly alter the constant term,\nthus making either a nearly correct equation that corresponds to the decrypted bit value of 0 or a\nfar-from-correct equation that corresponds to the decrypted bit value of 1. In the case of K-PKE,\nthe constant term is a polynomial with 256 coefficients, so one can encode more information:\none bit in each coefficient.\nTo this end, K-PKE.Encrypt proceeds by generating a vector 𝐲 ∈ 𝑅𝑞𝑘 and noise terms 𝐞𝟏 ∈ 𝑅𝑞𝑘\nand 𝑒2 ∈ 𝑅𝑞 , all of which are sampled from the centered binomial distribution using pseudoran-\ndomness expanded via PRF from the input randomness 𝑟. One then computes the “new noisy\nequation,” which is (up to some details) (𝐀⊺ 𝐲 + 𝐞1 , 𝐭⊺ 𝐲 + 𝑒2 ). An appropriate encoding 𝜇 of\nthe input message 𝑚 is then added to the latter term in the pair. Finally, the resulting pair (𝐮, 𝑣)\nis compressed, serialized into a byte array, and output as the ciphertext.\n\n5.3 K-PKE Decryption\nThe decryption algorithm K-PKE.Decrypt of K-PKE (Algorithm 15) takes a decryption key dkPKE\nand a ciphertext 𝑐 as input, requires no randomness, and outputs a plaintext 𝑚.\n\nInformal description. The algorithm K-PKE.Decrypt begins by recovering a pair (𝐮′ , 𝑣′ ) from the\nciphertext 𝑐 (see the description of K-PKE.Encrypt). Here, one can think of 𝐮′ as the coefficients\nof the equation and 𝑣′ as the constant term. The decryption key dkPKE contains the vector of\nsecret variables 𝐬. The decryption algorithm can thus use the decryption key to compute the\ntrue constant term 𝑣 = 𝐬⊺ 𝐮′ and calculate 𝑣′ − 𝑣. The decryption algorithm ends by decoding\nthe plaintext message 𝑚 from 𝑣′ − 𝑣 and outputting 𝑚.\n\nAlgorithm 15 K-PKE.Decrypt(dkPKE , 𝑐)\nUses the decryption key to decrypt a ciphertext.\nInput: decryption key dkPKE ∈ 𝔹384𝑘 .\nInput: ciphertext 𝑐 ∈ 𝔹32(𝑑𝑢 𝑘+𝑑𝑣 ) .\nOutput: message 𝑚 ∈ 𝔹32 .\n  1: 𝑐1 ← 𝑐[0 ∶ 32𝑑𝑢 𝑘]\n  2: 𝑐2 ← 𝑐[32𝑑𝑢 𝑘 ∶ 32(𝑑𝑢 𝑘 + 𝑑𝑣 )]\n  3: 𝐮′ ← Decompress𝑑 (ByteDecode𝑑 (𝑐1 )) ▷ run Decompress𝑑 and ByteDecode𝑑 𝑘 times\n                        𝑢                𝑢                 𝑢                  𝑢\n  4: 𝑣′ ← Decompress𝑑 (ByteDecode𝑑 (𝑐2 ))\n                        𝑣               𝑣\n  5: 𝐬 ̂ ← ByteDecode12 (dkPKE )                           ▷ run ByteDecode12 𝑘 times\n  6: 𝑤 ← 𝑣 − NTT (𝐬 ̂ ∘ NTT(𝐮 ))                   ▷ run NTT 𝑘 times; run NTT−1 once\n            ′       −1 ⊺              ′\n\n  7: 𝑚 ← ByteEncode1 (Compress1 (𝑤))             ▷ decode plaintext 𝑚 from polynomial 𝑣\n  8: return 𝑚\n\n\n\n\n                                                31\n\n\nFIPS 203                                     MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\n\n6.    Main Internal Algorithms\nThis section specifies three algorithms: ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal, ML-KEM.Encaps_internal,\nand ML-KEM.Decaps_internal. These three algorithms are all deterministic, meaning that their\noutput is completely determined by their input. No randomness is sampled inside of these\nalgorithms. These three algorithms will be used to construct ML-KEM in Section 7. The algorithms\nin this section make use of the parameters 𝑛, 𝑞, 𝑘, 𝑑𝑢 , and 𝑑𝑣 . The subroutines they invoke\nadditionally make use of the parameters 𝜂1 and 𝜂2 . While 𝑛 is always 256 and 𝑞 is always 3329,\nthe remaining parameters vary among the possible parameter sets (see Section 8).\nThe interfaces specified in this section will be used to test ML-KEM implementations through\nthe Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP). The key generation function in this\nsection may also be used to re-expand a key from a seed (see Section 3.3), including when\nobtaining assurance of private key possession via regeneration. As prescribed in Section 3.3, the\ninterfaces specified in this section should not be made available to applications other than for\ntesting purposes, and the random seeds (as specified in ML-KEM.KeyGen and ML-KEM.Encaps\nin Section 7) shall be generated by the cryptographic module.\n\n6.1 Internal Key Generation\nThe algorithm ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal (Algorithm 16) accepts two random seeds as input, and\nproduces an encapsulation key and a decapsulation key.\n\nInformal description. The core subroutine of ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal is the key generation\nalgorithm of K-PKE (Algorithm 13). The encapsulation key is simply the encryption key of K-PKE.\nThe decapsulation key consists of the decryption key of K-PKE, the encapsulation key, a hash\nof the encapsulation key, and a random 32-byte value. This random value will be used in the\n”implicit rejection” mechanism of the internal decapsulation algorithm (Algorithm 18).\n\nAlgorithm 16 ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal(𝑑, 𝑧)\nUses randomness to generate an encapsulation key and a corresponding decapsulation key.\nInput: randomness 𝑑 ∈ 𝔹32 .\nInput: randomness 𝑧 ∈ 𝔹32 .\nOutput: encapsulation key ek ∈ 𝔹384𝑘+32 .\nOutput: decapsulation key dk ∈ 𝔹768𝑘+96 .\n  1: (ekPKE , dkPKE ) ← K-PKE.KeyGen(𝑑)                       ▷ run key generation for K-PKE\n  2: ek ← ekPKE                                ▷ KEM encaps key is just the PKE encryption key\n  3: dk ← (dkPKE ‖ek‖H(ek)‖𝑧)                   ▷ KEM decaps key includes PKE decryption key\n  4: return (ek, dk)\n\n\n\n6.2 Internal Encapsulation\nThe algorithm ML-KEM.Encaps_internal (Algorithm 17) accepts an encapsulation key and a ran-\ndom byte array as input and outputs a ciphertext and a shared key.\n\n                                               32\n\n\nFIPS 203                                      MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\nAlgorithm 17 ML-KEM.Encaps_internal(ek, 𝑚)\nUses the encapsulation key and randomness to generate a key and an associated ciphertext.\nInput: encapsulation key ek ∈ 𝔹384𝑘+32 .\nInput: randomness 𝑚 ∈ 𝔹32 .\nOutput: shared secret key 𝐾 ∈ 𝔹32 .\nOutput: ciphertext 𝑐 ∈ 𝔹32(𝑑𝑢 𝑘+𝑑𝑣 ) .\n  1: (𝐾, 𝑟) ← G(𝑚‖H(ek))                        ▷ derive shared secret key 𝐾 and randomness 𝑟\n  2: 𝑐 ← K-PKE.Encrypt(ek, 𝑚, 𝑟)                   ▷ encrypt 𝑚 using K-PKE with randomness 𝑟\n  3: return (𝐾, 𝑐)\n\n\n\n\nInformal description. The core subroutine of ML-KEM.Encaps_internal is the encryption algo-\nrithm of K-PKE, which is used to encrypt a random value 𝑚 into a ciphertext 𝑐. A copy of the\nshared secret key 𝐾 and the randomness used during encryption are derived from 𝑚 and the\nencapsulation key ek via hashing. Specifically, H is applied to ek, and the result is concatenated\nwith 𝑚 and then hashed using G. Finally, the algorithm outputs the shared secret key 𝐾 and the\nciphertext 𝑐.\n\n6.3 Internal Decapsulation\nThe algorithm ML-KEM.Decaps_internal (Algorithm 18) accepts a decapsulation key and a cipher-\ntext as input, does not use any randomness, and outputs a shared secret key.\n\nInformal description. The algorithm ML-KEM.Decaps_internal begins by parsing out the com-\nponents of the decapsulation key dk of ML-KEM. These components are an (encryption key,\ndecryption key) pair for K-PKE, a hash value ℎ, and a random value 𝑧. The decryption key of\nK-PKE is then used to decrypt the input ciphertext 𝑐 to get a plaintext 𝑚′ . The decapsulation\nalgorithm then re-encrypts 𝑚′ and computes a candidate shared secret key 𝐾 ′ in the same\nmanner as should have been done in encapsulation. Specifically, 𝐾 ′ and the encryption ran-\ndomness 𝑟′ are computed by hashing 𝑚′ and the encryption key of K-PKE, and a ciphertext 𝑐′ is\ngenerated by encrypting 𝑚′ using randomness 𝑟′ . Finally, decapsulation checks whether the\nresulting ciphertext 𝑐′ matches the provided ciphertext 𝑐. If it does not, the algorithm performs\nan “implicit rejection”: the value of 𝐾 ′ is changed to a hash of 𝑐 together with the random value\n𝑧 stored in the ML-KEM secret key (see the discussion of decapsulation failures in Section 3.2).\nIn either case, decapsulation outputs the resulting shared secret key 𝐾 ′ .\nThe “implicit reject” flag computed in step 9 (by comparing 𝑐 and 𝑐′ ) is a secret piece of interme-\ndiate data. As specified in the requirements in Section 3.3, this flag shall be destroyed prior to\nML-KEM.Decaps_internal terminating. In particular, returning the value of the flag as an output\nin any form is not permitted.\n\n\n\n\n                                                33\n\n\nFIPS 203                                      MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\nAlgorithm 18 ML-KEM.Decaps_internal(dk, 𝑐)\nUses the decapsulation key to produce a shared secret key from a ciphertext.\nInput: decapsulation key dk ∈ 𝔹768𝑘+96 .\nInput: ciphertext 𝑐 ∈ 𝔹32(𝑑𝑢 𝑘+𝑑𝑣 ) .\nOutput: shared secret key 𝐾 ∈ 𝔹32 .\n  1: dkPKE ← dk[0 ∶ 384𝑘]                ▷ extract (from KEM decaps key) the PKE decryption key\n  2: ekPKE ← dk[384𝑘 ∶ 768𝑘 + 32]                                   ▷ extract PKE encryption key\n  3: ℎ ← dk[768𝑘 + 32 ∶ 768𝑘 + 64]                          ▷ extract hash of PKE encryption key\n  4: 𝑧 ← dk[768𝑘 + 64 ∶ 768𝑘 + 96]                              ▷ extract implicit rejection value\n  5: 𝑚′ ← K-PKE.Decrypt(dkPKE , 𝑐)                                          ▷ decrypt ciphertext\n  6: (𝐾 , 𝑟 ) ← G(𝑚 ‖ℎ)\n         ′ ′         ′\n\n  7: 𝐾̄ ← J(𝑧‖𝑐)\n  8: 𝑐′ ← K-PKE.Encrypt(ekPKE , 𝑚′ , 𝑟′ )          ▷ re-encrypt using the derived randomness 𝑟′\n  9: if 𝑐 ≠ 𝑐 ′ then\n10:       𝐾 ′ ← 𝐾̄                               ▷ if ciphertexts do not match, “implicitly reject”\n11: end if\n12: return 𝐾 ′\n\n\n\n\n                                                34\n\n\nFIPS 203                                     MODULE-LATTICE-BASED KEY-ENCAPSULATION MECHANISM\n\n\n\n7.      The ML-KEM Key-Encapsulation Mechanism\nThis section describes the three main algorithms of the ML-KEM scheme:\n     1. Key generation (ML-KEM.KeyGen)\n     2. Encapsulation (ML-KEM.Encaps)\n     3. Decapsulation (ML-KEM.Decaps)\nTo instantiate ML-KEM, one must select a parameter set. Each parameter set is associated with\na particular trade-off between security and performance. The three possible parameter sets are\ncalled ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024 and are described in detail in Table 2 of\nSection 8. Each parameter set assigns specific numerical values to the individual parameters 𝑛,\n𝑞, 𝑘, 𝜂1 , 𝜂2 , 𝑑𝑢 , and 𝑑𝑣 . While 𝑛 is always 256 and 𝑞 is always 3329, the remaining parameters\nvary among the three parameter sets. Implementers shall ensure that the three algorithms of\nML-KEM listed above are only invoked with a valid parameter set, and that this parameter set is\nselected appropriately for the desired application. Moreover, implementers shall ensure that the\nparameter set used in any particular invocation of ML-KEM.Encaps or ML-KEM.Decaps matches\nthe parameter set associated to the provided inputs.\n\n7.1 ML-KEM Key Generation\nThe key generation algorithm ML-KEM.KeyGen for ML-KEM (Algorithm 19) accepts no input,\ngenerates randomness internally, and produces an encapsulation key and a decapsulation key.\nWhile the encapsulation key can be made public, the decapsulation key shall remain private.\nThe seed (𝑑, 𝑧) generated in steps 1 and 2 of ML-KEM.KeyGen can be stored for later expan-\nsion using ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal (see Section 3.3). Can be any int16_t.\n * @param b Second factor. Must be signed canonical\n *          (abs value < (MLKEM_Q+1)/2).\n *\n * @return 16-bit integer congruent to a*b*R^{-1} mod MLKEM_Q, and\n *         smaller than MLKEM_Q in absolute value.\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE int16_t mlk_fqmul(int16_t a, int16_t b)\n__contract__(\n  requires(b > -MLKEM_Q_HALF && b < MLKEM_Q_HALF)\n  ensures(return_value > -MLKEM_Q && return_value < MLKEM_Q)\n)\n{\n  int16_t res;\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(&b, 1, MLKEM_Q_HALF);\n\n  res = mlk_montgomery_reduce((int32_t)a * (int32_t)b);\n  /* Bounds:\n   * |res| <= ceil(|a| * |b| / 2^16) + (MLKEM_Q + 1) / 2\n   *       <= ceil(2^15 * ((MLKEM_Q - 1)/2) / 2^16) + (MLKEM_Q + 1) / 2\n   *       <= ceil((MLKEM_Q - 1) / 4) + (MLKEM_Q + 1) / 2\n   *        < MLKEM_Q\n   */\n\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(&res, 1, MLKEM_Q);\n  return res;\n}\n\n/**\n * Barrett reduction; /* check-magic: 20159 == round(2^26 / MLKEM_Q) */\n\n  /*\n   * PORTABILITY: Right-shift on a signed integer is\n   * implementation-defined for negative left argument.\n   * Here, we assume it's sign-preserving \"arithmetic\" shift right.\n   * See (C99 6.5.7 (5))\n   */\n  const int32_t t = (magic * a + ((int32_t)1 << 25)) >> 26;\n\n  /*\n   * t is in -10 .. +10, so we need 32-bit math to\n   * evaluate t * MLKEM_Q and the subsequent subtraction\n   */\n  int16_t res = (int16_t)(a - t * MLKEM_Q);\n\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(&res, 1, MLKEM_Q_HALF);\n  return res;\n}\n\n/* Reference: `poly_tomont()` in the reference implementation @[REF]. */\nMLK_STATIC_TESTABLE void mlk_poly_tomont_c(mlk_poly *r)\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(r, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(r->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q))\n)\n{\n  unsigned i;\n  const int16_t f = 1353; This must be in\n *         Montgomery form and signed canonical.\n * - start: Offset to the beginning of the butterfly block\n * - len: Index difference between coefficients subject to a butterfly\n * - bound: Ghost variable describing coefficient bound: Prior to `start`,\n *          coefficients must be bound by `bound + MLKEM_Q`. Post `start`,\n *          they must be bound by `bound`.\n * When this function returns, output coefficients in the index range\n * [start, start+2*len) have bound bumped to `bound + MLKEM_Q`.\n * Example:\n * - start=8, len=4\n *   This would compute the following four butterflies\n *          8     --    12\n *             9    --     13\n *                10   --     14\n *                   11   --     15\n * - start=4, len=2\n *   This would compute the following two butterflies\n *          4 -- 6\n *             5 -- 7\n */\n\n/* Reference: Embedded in `ntt()` in the reference implementation @[REF]. */\nstatic void mlk_ntt_butterfly_block(int16_t r[MLKEM_N], int16_t zeta,\n                                    unsigned start, unsigned len,\n                                    unsigned bound)\n__contract__(\n  requires(start < MLKEM_N)\n  requires(1 <= len && len <= MLKEM_N / 2 && start + 2 * len <= MLKEM_N)\n  requires(0 <= bound && bound < INT16_MAX - MLKEM_Q)\n  requires(-MLKEM_Q_HALF < zeta && zeta < MLKEM_Q_HALF)\n  requires(memory_no_alias(r, sizeof(int16_t) * MLKEM_N))\n  requires(array_abs_bound(r, 0, start, bound + MLKEM_Q))\n  requires(array_abs_bound(r, start, MLKEM_N, bound))\n  assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(int16_t) * MLKEM_N))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(r, 0, start + 2*len, bound + MLKEM_Q))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(r, start + 2 * len, MLKEM_N, bound)))\n{\n  /* `bound` is a ghost variable only needed in the CBMC specification */\n  unsigned j;\n  ((void)bound);\n  for (j = start; j < start + len; j++)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(start <= j && j <= start + len)\n    /*\n     * Coefficients are updated in strided pairs, so the bounds for the\n     * intermediate states alternate twice between the old and new bound\n     */\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0,           j,           bound + MLKEM_Q))\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, j,           start + len, bound))\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, start + len, j + len,     bound + MLKEM_Q))\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, j + len,     MLKEM_N,     bound))\n    decreases(start + len - j))\n  {\n    int16_t t;\n    t = mlk_fqmul(r[j + len], zeta);\n    /* The precondition implies that the arithmetic does not overflow. */\n    r[j + len] = (int16_t)(r[j] - t);\n    r[j] = (int16_t)(r[j] + t);\n  }\n}\n\n/*\n * Compute one layer of forward NTT\n * Parameters:\n * - r: Pointer to base of polynomial\n * - layer: Variable indicating which layer is being applied.\n */\n\n/* Reference: Embedded in `ntt()` in the reference implementation @[REF]. */\nstatic void mlk_ntt_layer(int16_t r[MLKEM_N], unsigned layer)\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(r, sizeof(int16_t) * MLKEM_N))\n  requires(1 <= layer && layer <= 7)\n  requires(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, layer * MLKEM_Q))\n  assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(int16_t) * MLKEM_N))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, (layer + 1) * MLKEM_Q)))\n{\n  unsigned start, k, len;\n  /* Twiddle factors for layer n are at indices 2^(n-1)..2^n-1. */\n  k = 1u << (layer - 1);\n  len = (unsigned)MLKEM_N >> layer;\n  for (start = 0; start < MLKEM_N; start += 2 * len)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(start < MLKEM_N + 2 * len)\n    invariant(k <= MLKEM_N / 2 && 2 * len * k == start + MLKEM_N)\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0, start, layer * MLKEM_Q + MLKEM_Q))\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, start, MLKEM_N, layer * MLKEM_Q))\n    decreases(MLKEM_N - start))\n  {\n    int16_t zeta = mlk_zetas[k++];\n    mlk_ntt_butterfly_block(r, zeta, start, len, layer * MLKEM_Q);\n  }\n}\n\n/*\n * Compute full forward NTT\n * NOTE: This particular implementation satisfies a much tighter\n * bound on the output coefficients (5*q) than the contractual one (8*q),\n * but this is not needed in the calling code. Should we change the\n * base multiplication strategy to require smaller NTT output bounds,\n * the proof may need strengthening.\n */\n\n/* Reference: `ntt()` in the reference implementation @[REF].\n * - Iterate over `layer` instead of `len` in the outer loop\n *   to simplify computation of zeta index. */\nMLK_STATIC_TESTABLE void mlk_poly_ntt_c(mlk_poly *p)\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(p, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  requires(array_abs_bound(p->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q))\n  assigns(memory_slice(p, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(p->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLK_NTT_BOUND))\n)\n{\n  unsigned layer;\n  int16_t *r;\n\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(p, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q);\n\n  r = p->coeffs;\n\n  for (layer = 1; layer <= 7; layer++)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(1 <= layer && layer <= 8)\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, layer * MLKEM_Q))\n    decreases(8 - layer))\n  {\n    mlk_ntt_layer(r, layer);\n  }\n\n  /* Check the stronger bound */\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(p, MLKEM_N, MLK_NTT_BOUND);\n}\n\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nvoid mlk_poly_ntt(mlk_poly *r)\n{\n#if defined(MLK_USE_NATIVE_NTT)\n  int ret;\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(r, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q);\n  ret = mlk_ntt_native(r->coeffs);\n  if (ret == MLK_NATIVE_FUNC_SUCCESS)\n  {\n    mlk_assert_abs_bound(r, MLKEM_N, MLK_NTT_BOUND);\n    return;\n  }\n#endif /* MLK_USE_NATIVE_NTT */\n\n  mlk_poly_ntt_c(r);\n}\n\n\n/* Compute one layer of inverse NTT */\n\n/* Reference: Embedded into `invntt()` in the reference implementation @[REF] */\nstatic void mlk_invntt_layer(int16_t *r, unsigned layer)\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(r, sizeof(int16_t) * MLKEM_N))\n  requires(1 <= layer && layer <= 7)\n  requires(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q))\n  assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(int16_t) * MLKEM_N))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q)))\n{\n  unsigned start, k, len;\n  len = (unsigned)MLKEM_N >> layer;\n  k = (1u << layer) - 1;\n  for (start = 0; start < MLKEM_N; start += 2 * len)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q))\n    invariant(start <= MLKEM_N && k <= 127)\n    /* Normalised form of k == MLKEM_N / len - 1 - start / (2 * len) */\n    invariant(2 * len * k + start == 2 * MLKEM_N - 2 * len)\n    decreases(MLKEM_N - start))\n  {\n    unsigned j;\n    int16_t zeta = mlk_zetas[k--];\n    for (j = start; j < start + len; j++)\n    __loop__(\n      invariant(start <= j && j <= start + len)\n      invariant(start <= MLKEM_N && k <= 127)\n      invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q))\n      decreases(start + len - j))\n    {\n      int16_t t = r[j];\n      /* The preconditions imply that the arithmetic does not overflow. */\n      r[j] = mlk_barrett_reduce((int16_t)(t + r[j + len]));\n      r[j + len] = (int16_t)(r[j + len] - t);\n      r[j + len] = mlk_fqmul(r[j + len], zeta);\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n/* Reference: `invntt()` in the reference implementation @[REF]\n *            - We normalize at the beginning of the inverse NTT,\n *              while the reference implementation normalizes at\n *              the end. This allows us to drop a call to `poly_reduce()`\n *              from the base multiplication. */\nMLK_STATIC_TESTABLE void mlk_poly_invntt_tomont_c(mlk_poly *p)\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(p, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  assigns(memory_slice(p, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(p->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLK_INVNTT_BOUND))\n)\n{\n  unsigned j, layer;\n  const int16_t f = 1441; /* check-magic: 1441 == pow(2,32 - 7,MLKEM_Q) */\n  int16_t *r = p->coeffs;\n\n  /*\n   * Scale input polynomial to account for Montgomery factor\n   * and NTT twist. This also brings coefficients down to\n   * absolute value < MLKEM_Q.\n   */\n  for (j = 0; j < MLKEM_N; j++)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(j <= MLKEM_N)\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0, j, MLKEM_Q))\n    decreases(MLKEM_N - j))\n  {\n    r[j] = mlk_fqmul(r[j], f);\n  }\n\n  /* Run the invNTT layers */\n  for (layer = 7; layer > 0; layer--)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(0 <= layer && layer < 8)\n    invariant(array_abs_bound(r, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_Q))\n    decreases(layer))\n  {\n    mlk_invntt_layer(r, layer);\n  }\n\n  mlk_assert_abs_bound(p, MLKEM_N, MLK_INVNTT_BOUND);\n}\n\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nvoid mlk_poly_invntt_tomont(mlk_poly *r)\n{\n#if defined(MLK_USE_NATIVE_INTT)\n  int ret;\n  ret = mlk_intt_native(r->coeffs);\n  if (ret == MLK_NATIVE_FUNC_SUCCESS)\n  {\n    mlk_assert_abs_bound(r, MLKEM_N, MLK_INVNTT_BOUND);\n    return;\n  }\n#endif /* MLK_USE_NATIVE_INTT */\n\n  mlk_poly_invntt_tomont_c(r);\n}\n\n#else /* !MLK_CONFIG_MULTILEVEL_NO_SHARED */\n\nMLK_EMPTY_CU(mlk_poly)\n\n#endif /* MLK_CONFIG_MULTILEVEL_NO_SHARED */\n\n----- content end -----\n===== RAW_PRIMARY_EVIDENCE FILE END =====\n\n\n===== RAW_PRIMARY_EVIDENCE FILE BEGIN =====\ntrust_boundary: highest_priority_for_stage_claims\npath: /home/girish/thesis-repos/mlkem-native/mlkem/src/poly.h\nname: poly.h\nsize_bytes: 10117\n----- content begin -----\n/*\n * Copyright (c) The mlkem-native project authors\n * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT\n */\n\n/* References\n * ==========\n *\n * - [FIPS203]\n *   FIPS 203 Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard\n *   National Institute of Standards and Technology\n *   https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final\n */\n\n#ifndef MLK_POLY_H\n#define MLK_POLY_H\n\n\n#include \"cbmc.h\"\n#include \"common.h\"\n#include \"debug.h\"\n#include \"verify.h\"\n\n/* Absolute exclusive upper bound for the output of the inverse NTT */\n#define MLK_INVNTT_BOUND (8 * MLKEM_Q)\n\n/* Absolute exclusive upper bound for the output of the forward NTT */\n#define MLK_NTT_BOUND (8 * MLKEM_Q)\n\n/**\n * Element of R_q = Z_q[X]/(X^n + 1). j < 8; j++)\n    __loop__(\n      invariant(j <= 8 && i <= MLKEM_N / 8)\n      invariant(array_bound(r->coeffs, 0, 8 * i + j, 0, MLKEM_Q))\n      decreases(8 - j))\n    {\n      r->coeffs[8 * i + j] = mlk_scalar_decompress_d5(t[j]);\n    }\n  }\n\n  mlk_assert_bound(r, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q);\n}\n\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nvoid mlk_poly_decompress_d5(mlk_poly *r,\n                            const uint8_t a[MLKEM_POLYCOMPRESSEDBYTES_D5])\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(r, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(a, MLKEM_POLYCOMPRESSEDBYTES_D5))\n  assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  ensures(array_bound(r->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q))\n)\n{\n#if defined(MLK_USE_NATIVE_POLY_DECOMPRESS_D5)\n  int ret;\n  ret = mlk_poly_decompress_d5_native(r->coeffs, a);\n  if (ret == MLK_NATIVE_FUNC_SUCCESS)\n  {\n    mlk_assert_bound(r, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q);\n    return;\n  }\n#endif /* MLK_USE_NATIVE_POLY_DECOMPRESS_D5 */\n\n  mlk_poly_decompress_d5_c(r, a);\n}\n\n/* Reference: Embedded into `polyvec_decompress()` in the\n *            reference implementation, for ML-KEM-1024. */\nMLK_STATIC_TESTABLE void mlk_poly_decompress_d11_c(\n    mlk_poly *r, const uint8_t a[MLKEM_POLYCOMPRESSEDBYTES_D11])\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(r, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(a, MLKEM_POLYCOMPRESSEDBYTES_D11))\n  assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  ensures(array_bound(r->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q))\n)\n{\n  unsigned j;\n  for (j = 0; Coefficients\n *                      will be normalized to [0,1,..,MLKEM_Q-1].\n * @param[out] seed     Output seed to generate matrix A.\n * @param[in]  packedpk Input serialized public key.\n */\nstatic void mlk_unpack_pk(mlk_polyvec *pk, uint8_t seed[MLKEM_SYMBYTES],\n                          const uint8_t packedpk[MLKEM_INDCPA_PUBLICKEYBYTES])\n{\n  mlk_polyvec_frombytes(pk, packedpk);\n  mlk_memcpy(seed, packedpk + MLKEM_POLYVECBYTES, MLKEM_SYMBYTES);\n\n  /* NOTE: If a modulus check was conducted on the PK, we know at this\n   * point that the coefficients of `pk` are unsigned canonical. The\n   * specifications and proofs, however, do _not_ assume this, and instead\n   * work with the easily provable bound by MLKEM_UINT12_LIMIT. */\n}\n\n/**\n * Serialize the secret key.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Algorithm 13 (K-PKE.KeyGen), L20].}\n *\n * @param[out] r  Output serialized secret key.\n * @param[in]  sk Input vector of polynomials (secret key).\n */\nstatic void mlk_pack_sk(uint8_t r[MLKEM_INDCPA_SECRETKEYBYTES],\n                        const mlk_polyvec *sk)\n{\n  mlk_assert_bound_2d(sk->vec, MLKEM_K, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q);\n  mlk_polyvec_tobytes(r, sk);\n}\n\n/**\n * De-serialize the secret key; inverse of mlk_pack_sk.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Algorithm 15 (K-PKE.Decrypt), L5].}\n *\n * @param[out] sk       Output vector of polynomials (secret key).\n * @param[in]  packedsk Input serialized secret key.\n */\nstatic void mlk_unpack_sk(mlk_polyvec *sk,\n                          const uint8_t packedsk[MLKEM_INDCPA_SECRETKEYBYTES])\n{\n  mlk_polyvec_frombytes(sk, packedsk);\n}\n\n/**\n * Serialize the ciphertext as the concatenation of the compressed and\n * serialized vector of polynomials b and the compressed and serialized\n * polynomial v.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Algorithm 14 (K-PKE.Encrypt), L22-23].}\n *\n * @param[out] r Output serialized ciphertext.\n * @param[in]  b Input vector of polynomials b.\n * @param[in]  v Input polynomial v.\n */\nstatic void mlk_pack_ciphertext(uint8_t r[MLKEM_INDCPA_BYTES],\n                                const mlk_polyvec *b, mlk_poly *v)\n{\n  mlk_polyvec_compress_du(r, b);\n  mlk_poly_compress_dv(r + MLKEM_POLYVECCOMPRESSEDBYTES_DU, v);\n}\n\n/**\n * De-serialize and decompress ciphertext from a byte array; approximate\n * inverse of mlk_pack_ciphertext.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Algorithm 15 (K-PKE.Decrypt), L1-4].}\n *\n * @param[out] b Output vector of polynomials b.\n * @param[out] v Output polynomial v.\n * @param[in]  c Input serialized ciphertext.\n */\nstatic void mlk_unpack_ciphertext(mlk_polyvec *b, mlk_poly *v,\n                                  const uint8_t c[MLKEM_INDCPA_BYTES])\n{\n  mlk_polyvec_decompress_du(b, c);\n  mlk_poly_decompress_dv(v, c + MLKEM_POLYVECCOMPRESSEDBYTES_DU);\n}\n\n/* Helper function to ensure that the polynomial entries in the output\n * of gen_matrix use the standard (bitreversed) ordering of coefficients.\n * No-op unless a native backend with a custom ordering is used.\n *\n * We don't inline this into gen_matrix to avoid having to split the CBMC\n * proof for gen_matrix based on MLK_USE_NATIVE_NTT_CUSTOM_ORDER. */\nstatic void mlk_polyvec_permute_bitrev_to_custom(mlk_polyvec *v)\n__contract__(\n  /* We don't specify that this should be a permutation, but only\n   * that it does not change the bound established at the end of mlk_gen_matrix. */\n  requires(memory_no_alias(v, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(forall(x, 0, MLKEM_K,\n    array_bound(v->vec[x].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q)))\n  assigns(memory_slice(v, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  ensures(forall(x, 0, MLKEM_K,\n    array_bound(v->vec[x].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q))))\n{\n#if defined(MLK_USE_NATIVE_NTT_CUSTOM_ORDER)\n  unsigned i;\n  for (i = 0; i < MLKEM_K; i++)\n  __loop__(\n     assigns(i, memory_slice(v, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n     invariant(i <= MLKEM_K)\n     invariant(forall(x, 0, MLKEM_K,\n       array_bound(v->vec[x].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q)))\n     decreases(MLKEM_K - i))\n  {\n    mlk_poly_permute_bitrev_to_custom(v->vec[i].coeffs);\n  }\n#else  /* MLK_USE_NATIVE_NTT_CUSTOM_ORDER */\n  /* Nothing to do */\n  (void)v;\n#endif /* !MLK_USE_NATIVE_NTT_CUSTOM_ORDER */\n}\n\nstatic void mlk_polymat_permute_bitrev_to_custom(mlk_polymat *a)\n__contract__(\n  /* We don't specify that this should be a permutation, but only\n   * that it does not change the bound established at the end of mlk_gen_matrix. */\n  requires(memory_no_alias(a, sizeof(mlk_polymat)))\n  requires(forall(x, 0, MLKEM_K, forall(y, 0, MLKEM_K,\n    array_bound(a->vec[x].vec[y].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q))))\n  assigns(memory_slice(a, sizeof(mlk_polymat)))\n  ensures(forall(x, 0, MLKEM_K, forall(y, 0, MLKEM_K,\n    array_bound(a->vec[x].vec[y].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q)))))\n{\n  unsigned i;\n  for (i = 0; i < MLKEM_K; i++)\n  __loop__(\n     assigns(i, memory_slice(a, sizeof(mlk_polymat)))\n     invariant(i <= MLKEM_K)\n     invariant(forall(x, 0, MLKEM_K, forall(y, 0, MLKEM_K,\n       array_bound(a->vec[x].vec[y].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_Q))))\n     decreases(MLKEM_K - i))\n  {\n    mlk_polyvec_permute_bitrev_to_custom(&a->vec[i]);\n  }\n}\n\n/* Reference: `gen_matrix()` in the reference implementation @[REF].\n *            - We use a special subroutine to generate 4 polynomials\n *              at a time, to be able to leverage batched Keccak-f1600\n *              implementations. The reference implementation generates\n *              one matrix entry a time.\n *\n * Not static for benchmarking */\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nvoid mlk_gen_matrix(mlk_polymat *a, const uint8_t seed[MLKEM_SYMBYTES],\n                    int transposed)\n{\n  unsigned i, j;\n  MLK_ALIGN uint8_t seed_ext[4][MLK_ALIGN_UP(MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 2)];\n\n  for (j = 0; j < 4; j++)\n  {\n    mlk_memcpy(seed_ext[j], seed, MLKEM_SYMBYTES);\n  }\n\n#if !defined(MLK_CONFIG_SERIAL_FIPS202_ONLY)\n  /* Sample 4 matrix entries a time. */\n  for (i = 0; i < (MLKEM_K * MLKEM_K / 4) * 4; i += 4)\n  {\n    for (j = 0; j < 4; j++)\n    {\n      uint8_t x, y;\n      /* MLKEM_K <= 4, so the values fit in uint8_t. */\n      x = (uint8_t)((i + j) / MLKEM_K);\n      y = (uint8_t)((i + j) % MLKEM_K);\n      if (transposed)\n      {\n        seed_ext[j][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 0] = x;\n        seed_ext[j][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1] = y;\n      }\n      else\n      {\n        seed_ext[j][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 0] = y;\n        seed_ext[j][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1] = x;\n      }\n    }\n\n    mlk_poly_rej_uniform_x4(&a->vec[i / MLKEM_K].vec[i % MLKEM_K],\n                            &a->vec[(i + 1) / MLKEM_K].vec[(i + 1) % MLKEM_K],\n                            &a->vec[(i + 2) / MLKEM_K].vec[(i + 2) % MLKEM_K],\n                            &a->vec[(i + 3) / MLKEM_K].vec[(i + 3) % MLKEM_K],\n                            seed_ext);\n  }\n#else  /* !MLK_CONFIG_SERIAL_FIPS202_ONLY */\n  /* When using serial FIPS202, sample all entries individually. */\n  i = 0;\n#endif /* MLK_CONFIG_SERIAL_FIPS202_ONLY */\n\n  /* For MLKEM_K == 3, sample the last entry individually.\n   * When MLK_CONFIG_SERIAL_FIPS202_ONLY is set, sample all entries\n   * individually. */\n  for (; i < MLKEM_K * MLKEM_K; i++)\n  {\n    uint8_t x, y;\n    /* MLKEM_K <= 4, so the values fit in uint8_t. */\n    x = (uint8_t)(i / MLKEM_K);\n    y = (uint8_t)(i % MLKEM_K);\n\n    if (transposed)\n    {\n      seed_ext[0][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 0] = x;\n      seed_ext[0][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1] = y;\n    }\n    else\n    {\n      seed_ext[0][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 0] = y;\n      seed_ext[0][MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1] = x;\n    }\n\n    mlk_poly_rej_uniform(&a->vec[i / MLKEM_K].vec[i % MLKEM_K], seed_ext[0]);\n  }\n\n  mlk_assert(i == MLKEM_K * MLKEM_K);\n\n  /*\n   * The public matrix is generated in NTT domain. If the native backend\n   * uses a custom order in NTT domain, permute A accordingly.\n   */\n  mlk_polymat_permute_bitrev_to_custom(a);\n\n  /* Specification: Partially implements\n   * @[FIPS203, Section 3.3, Destruction of intermediate values] */\n  mlk_zeroize(seed_ext, sizeof(seed_ext));\n}\n\n/**\n * Compute matrix-vector product in NTT domain, via Montgomery multiplication.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Section 2.4.7, Eq (2.12), (2.13)].}\n *\n * @param[out] out Output polynomial vector.\n * @param[in]  a   Input matrix. Must be in NTT domain and have coefficients\n *                 of absolute value < 4096.\n * @param[in]  v   Input polynomial vector. Must be in NTT domain.\n * @param[in]  vc  Mulcache for @p v, computed via\n *                 mlk_polyvec_mulcache_compute().\n */\nstatic void mlk_matvec_mul(mlk_polyvec *out, const mlk_polymat *a,\n                           const mlk_polyvec *v, const mlk_polyvec_mulcache *vc)\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(out, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(a, sizeof(mlk_polymat)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(v, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(vc, sizeof(mlk_polyvec_mulcache)))\n  requires(forall(k0, 0, MLKEM_K,\n    forall(k1, 0, MLKEM_K,\n      array_bound(a->vec[k0].vec[k1].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, 0, MLKEM_UINT12_LIMIT))))\n  assigns(memory_slice(out, sizeof(mlk_polyvec))))\n{\n  unsigned i;\n  for (i = 0; i < MLKEM_K; i++)\n  __loop__(\n    assigns(i, memory_slice(out, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n    invariant(i <= MLKEM_K)\n    decreases(MLKEM_K - i))\n  {\n    mlk_polyvec_basemul_acc_montgomery_cached(&out->vec[i], &a->vec[i], v, vc);\n  }\n}\n\n/**\n * Compute and fill the pv and e polyvec structures needed by\n * mlk_keypair_derand(). Uses x4-batched versions of `poly_getnoise` to\n * leverage batched Keccak-f1600.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Algorithm 13 (K-PKE.KeyGen)] steps 8-15.}\n *\n * @param[out] pv   Output polynomial vector.\n * @param[out] e    Output polynomial vector.\n * @param[in]  seed Seed bytes for sampling.\n */\nstatic void mlk_keypair_getnoise_eta1(mlk_polyvec *pv, mlk_polyvec *e,\n                                      const uint8_t seed[MLKEM_SYMBYTES])\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(pv, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(e, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(seed, MLKEM_SYMBYTES))\n  assigns(memory_slice(pv, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  assigns(memory_slice(e, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  ensures(forall(k0, 0, MLKEM_K, array_abs_bound(pv->vec[k0].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_ETA1 + 1)))\n  ensures(forall(k1, 0, MLKEM_K, array_abs_bound(e->vec[k1].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_ETA1 + 1)))\n)\n{\n#if MLKEM_K == 2\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&pv->vec[0], &pv->vec[1], /* Fill elements of pv */\n                            &e->vec[0], &e->vec[1], /* and two elements of e */\n                            seed, 0, 1, 2, 3);\n#elif MLKEM_K == 3\n  /*\n   * Only the first three output buffers are needed, so we pass NULL as\n   * the fourth parameter, and 0xFF as its dummy nonce.\n   */\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&pv->vec[0], &pv->vec[1], &pv->vec[2], NULL, seed,\n                            0, 1, 2, 0xFF);\n  /* Same here */\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&e->vec[0], &e->vec[1], &e->vec[2], NULL, seed, 3,\n                            4, 5, 0xFF);\n#elif MLKEM_K == 4\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&pv->vec[0], &pv->vec[1], &pv->vec[2], &pv->vec[3],\n                            seed, 0, 1, 2, 3);\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&e->vec[0], &e->vec[1], &e->vec[2], &e->vec[3],\n                            seed, 4, 5, 6, 7);\n#endif /* MLKEM_K == 4 */\n}\n\n/**\n * Compute and fill the sp, ep, and epp polynomial structures needed by\n * mlk_indcpa_enc(). Uses x4-batched versions of `poly_getnoise` to leverage\n * batched Keccak-f1600.\n *\n * @spec{Implements @[FIPS203, Algorithm 14 (K-PKE.Encrypt)] steps 9-16.}\n *\n * @param[out] sp    Output polynomial vector.\n * @param[out] ep    Output polynomial vector.\n * @param[out] epp   Output polynomial.\n * @param[in]  coins Seed bytes for sampling.\n */\nstatic void mlk_enc_getnoise_eta1_eta2(mlk_polyvec *sp, mlk_polyvec *ep,\n                                       mlk_poly *epp,\n                                       const uint8_t coins[MLKEM_SYMBYTES])\n__contract__(\n  requires(memory_no_alias(sp, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(ep, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(epp, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(coins, MLKEM_SYMBYTES))\n  assigns(memory_slice(sp, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  assigns(memory_slice(ep, sizeof(mlk_polyvec)))\n  assigns(memory_slice(epp, sizeof(mlk_poly)))\n  ensures(forall(k0, 0, MLKEM_K, array_abs_bound(sp->vec[k0].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_ETA1 + 1)))\n  ensures(forall(k1, 0, MLKEM_K, array_abs_bound(ep->vec[k1].coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_ETA2 + 1)))\n  ensures(array_abs_bound(epp->coeffs, 0, MLKEM_N, MLKEM_ETA2 + 1))\n)\n{\n#if MLKEM_K == 2\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1122_4x(&sp->vec[0], &sp->vec[1], &ep->vec[0],\n                               &ep->vec[1], coins, 0, 1, 2, 3);\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta2(epp, coins, 4);\n#elif MLKEM_K == 3\n  /*\n   * In this call, only the first three output buffers are needed,\n   * so we pass NULL as the fourth parameter, and 0xFF as its dummy nonce.\n   */\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&sp->vec[0], &sp->vec[1], &sp->vec[2], NULL, coins,\n                            0, 1, 2, 0xFF /* irrelevant */);\n  /* The fourth output buffer in this call _is_ used. */\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta2_4x(&ep->vec[0], &ep->vec[1], &ep->vec[2], epp, coins,\n                            3, 4, 5, 6);\n#elif MLKEM_K == 4\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta1_4x(&sp->vec[0], &sp->vec[1], &sp->vec[2], &sp->vec[3],\n                            coins, 0, 1, 2, 3);\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta2_4x(&ep->vec[0], &ep->vec[1], &ep->vec[2], &ep->vec[3],\n                            coins, 4, 5, 6, 7);\n  mlk_poly_getnoise_eta2(epp, coins, 8);\n#endif /* MLKEM_K == 4 */\n}\n\n\n/* Reference: `indcpa_keypair_derand()` in the reference implementation @[REF].\n *            - We use a different implementation of `gen_matrix()` which\n *              uses x4-batched Keccak-f1600 (see `mlk_gen_matrix()` above).\n *            - We use a mulcache to speed up matrix-vector multiplication.\n *            - We include buffer zeroization.\n */\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nint mlk_indcpa_keypair_derand(uint8_t pk[MLKEM_INDCPA_PUBLICKEYBYTES],\n                              uint8_t sk[MLKEM_INDCPA_SECRETKEYBYTES],\n                              const uint8_t coins[MLKEM_SYMBYTES],\n                              MLK_CONFIG_CONTEXT_PARAMETER_TYPE context)\n{\n  int ret = 0;\n  const uint8_t *publicseed;\n  const uint8_t *noiseseed;\n  MLK_ALLOC(buf, uint8_t, 2 * MLKEM_SYMBYTES, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(coins_with_domain_separator, uint8_t, MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(a, mlk_polymat, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(e, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(pkpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(skpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(skpv_cache, mlk_polyvec_mulcache, 1, context);\n\n  if (buf == NULL || coins_with_domain_separator == NULL || a == NULL ||\n      e == NULL || pkpv == NULL || skpv == NULL || skpv_cache == NULL)\n  {\n    ret = MLK_ERR_OUT_OF_MEMORY;\n    goto cleanup;\n  }\n\n  publicseed = buf;\n  noiseseed = buf + MLKEM_SYMBYTES;\n\n  /* Concatenate coins with MLKEM_K for domain separation of security levels */\n  mlk_memcpy(coins_with_domain_separator, coins, MLKEM_SYMBYTES);\n  coins_with_domain_separator[MLKEM_SYMBYTES] = MLKEM_K;\n\n  mlk_hash_g(buf, coins_with_domain_separator, MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1);\n\n  /*\n   * Declassify the public seed.\n   * Required to use it in conditional-branches in rejection sampling.\n   * This is needed because all output of randombytes is marked as secret\n   * (=undefined)\n   */\n  MLK_CT_TESTING_DECLASSIFY(publicseed, MLKEM_SYMBYTES);\n\n  mlk_gen_matrix(a, publicseed, 0 /* no transpose */);\n\n  mlk_keypair_getnoise_eta1(skpv, e, noiseseed);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_ntt(skpv);\n  mlk_polyvec_ntt(e);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_mulcache_compute(skpv_cache, skpv);\n  mlk_matvec_mul(pkpv, a, skpv, skpv_cache);\n  mlk_polyvec_tomont(pkpv);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_add(pkpv, e);\n  mlk_polyvec_reduce(pkpv);\n  mlk_polyvec_reduce(skpv);\n\n  mlk_pack_sk(sk, skpv);\n  mlk_pack_pk(pk, pkpv, publicseed);\n\ncleanup:\n  /* Specification: Partially implements\n   * @[FIPS203, Section 3.3, Destruction of intermediate values] */\n  MLK_FREE(skpv_cache, mlk_polyvec_mulcache, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(skpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(pkpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(e, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(a, mlk_polymat, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(coins_with_domain_separator, uint8_t, MLKEM_SYMBYTES + 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(buf, uint8_t, 2 * MLKEM_SYMBYTES, context);\n  return ret;\n}\n\n/* Reference: `indcpa_enc()` in the reference implementation @[REF].\n *            - We use x4-batched versions of `poly_getnoise` to leverage\n *              batched x4-batched Keccak-f1600.\n *            - We use a different implementation of `gen_matrix()` which\n *              uses x4-batched Keccak-f1600 (see `mlk_gen_matrix()` above).\n *            - We use a mulcache to speed up matrix-vector multiplication.\n *            - We include buffer zeroization.\n */\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nint mlk_indcpa_enc(uint8_t c[MLKEM_INDCPA_BYTES],\n                   const uint8_t m[MLKEM_INDCPA_MSGBYTES],\n                   const uint8_t pk[MLKEM_INDCPA_PUBLICKEYBYTES],\n                   const uint8_t coins[MLKEM_SYMBYTES],\n                   MLK_CONFIG_CONTEXT_PARAMETER_TYPE context)\n{\n  int ret = 0;\n  MLK_ALLOC(seed, uint8_t, MLKEM_SYMBYTES, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(at, mlk_polymat, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(sp, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(pkpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(ep, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(b, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(v, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(k, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(epp, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(sp_cache, mlk_polyvec_mulcache, 1, context);\n\n  if (seed == NULL || at == NULL || sp == NULL || pkpv == NULL || ep == NULL ||\n      b == NULL || v == NULL || k == NULL || epp == NULL || sp_cache == NULL)\n  {\n    ret = MLK_ERR_OUT_OF_MEMORY;\n    goto cleanup;\n  }\n\n  mlk_unpack_pk(pkpv, seed, pk);\n  mlk_poly_frommsg(k, m);\n\n  /*\n   * Declassify the public seed.\n   * Required to use it in conditional-branches in rejection sampling.\n   * This is needed because in re-encryption the publicseed originated from sk\n   * which is marked undefined.\n   */\n  MLK_CT_TESTING_DECLASSIFY(seed, MLKEM_SYMBYTES);\n\n  mlk_gen_matrix(at, seed, 1 /* transpose */);\n\n  mlk_enc_getnoise_eta1_eta2(sp, ep, epp, coins);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_ntt(sp);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_mulcache_compute(sp_cache, sp);\n  mlk_matvec_mul(b, at, sp, sp_cache);\n  mlk_polyvec_basemul_acc_montgomery_cached(v, pkpv, sp, sp_cache);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_invntt_tomont(b);\n  mlk_poly_invntt_tomont(v);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_add(b, ep);\n  mlk_poly_add(v, epp);\n  mlk_poly_add(v, k);\n\n  mlk_polyvec_reduce(b);\n  mlk_poly_reduce(v);\n\n  mlk_pack_ciphertext(c, b, v);\n\ncleanup:\n  /* Specification: Partially implements\n   * @[FIPS203, Section 3.3, Destruction of intermediate values] */\n  MLK_FREE(sp_cache, mlk_polyvec_mulcache, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(epp, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(k, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(v, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(b, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(ep, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(pkpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(sp, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(at, mlk_polymat, 1, context);\n  MLK_FREE(seed, uint8_t, MLKEM_SYMBYTES, context);\n  return ret;\n}\n\n/* Reference: `indcpa_dec()` in the reference implementation @[REF].\n *            - We use a mulcache for the scalar product.\n *            - We include buffer zeroization. */\nMLK_INTERNAL_API\nint mlk_indcpa_dec(uint8_t m[MLKEM_INDCPA_MSGBYTES],\n                   const uint8_t c[MLKEM_INDCPA_BYTES],\n                   const uint8_t sk[MLKEM_INDCPA_SECRETKEYBYTES],\n                   MLK_CONFIG_CONTEXT_PARAMETER_TYPE context)\n{\n  int ret = 0;\n  MLK_ALLOC(b, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(skpv, mlk_polyvec, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(v, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(sb, mlk_poly, 1, context);\n  MLK_ALLOC(b_cache, mlk_polyvec_mulcache, 1, context);\n\n  if (b == NULL || skpv == NULL || v == NULL || sb == NULL || b_cache == NULL)\n  {\n    ret = MLK_ERR_OUT_OF_MEMORY;\n    goto cleanup;\n  }\n\n  mlk_unpack_ciphertext(b, v, c);\n  mlk_unpack_sk(skpv, @[REF]. Used as part of signed->unsigned\n * conversion for modular representatives to detect whether the input is\n * negative. This happens in `mlk_poly_reduce()` here, and as part of\n * polynomial compression functions in the reference implementation. See\n * `mlk_poly_reduce()`. We use value barriers to reduce the risk of\n * compiler-introduced branches.}\n *\n * @param x Value to be converted into a mask.\n *\n * @return Mask value (0 or 0xFFFF).\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE uint16_t mlk_ct_cmask_neg_i16(int16_t x)\n__contract__(ensures(return_value == ((x < 0) ? 0xFFFF : 0)))\n{\n  int32_t tmp = mlk_value_barrier_i32((int32_t)x);\n  /*\n   * PORTABILITY: Right-shift on a signed integer is\n   * implementation-defined for negative left argument.\n   * Here, we assume it's sign-preserving \"arithmetic\" shift right.\n   * See (C99 6.5.7 (5))\n   */\n  tmp >>= 16;\n  return mlk_cast_int32_to_uint16(tmp);\n}\n\n/**\n * Return 0 if input is zero, and -1 otherwise.\n *\n * @reference{Embedded in `cmov_int16()` in the reference implementation\n * @[REF]. Uses a value barrier and shift instead of `b = -b` to convert\n * condition into mask.}\n *\n * @param x Value to be converted into a mask.\n *\n * @return Mask value (0 or 0xFFFF).\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE uint16_t mlk_ct_cmask_nonzero_u16(uint16_t x)\n__contract__(ensures(return_value == ((x == 0) ? 0 : 0xFFFF)))\n{\n  int32_t tmp = mlk_value_barrier_i32(-((int32_t)x));\n  /*\n   * PORTABILITY: Right-shift on a signed integer is\n   * implementation-defined for negative left argument.\n   * Here, we assume it's sign-preserving \"arithmetic\" shift right.\n   * See (C99 6.5.7 (5))\n   */\n  tmp >>= 16;\n  return mlk_cast_int32_to_uint16(tmp);\n}\n\n/**\n * Return 0 if input is zero, and -1 otherwise.\n *\n * @reference{Embedded in `verify()` and `cmov()` in the reference\n * implementation @[REF]. We include a value barrier not present in the\n * reference implementation, to prevent the compiler from realizing that\n * this function returns a mask.}\n *\n * @param x Value to be converted into a mask.\n *\n * @return Mask value (0 or 0xFF).\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE uint8_t mlk_ct_cmask_nonzero_u8(uint8_t x)\n__contract__(ensures(return_value == ((x == 0) ? 0 : 0xFF)))\n{\n  uint16_t mask = mlk_ct_cmask_nonzero_u16((uint16_t)x);\n  return (uint8_t)(mask & 0xFF);\n}\n\n/**\n * Functionally equivalent to cond ? a : b, but implemented with guards\n * against compiler-introduced branches.\n *\n * @spec{With `a = MLKEM_Q_HALF` and `b=0`, this essentially implements\n * `Decompress_1` @[FIPS203, Eq (4.8)] in `mlk_poly_frommsg()`. With\n * `a = x + MLKEM_Q`, `b = x`, and `cond` indicating whether `x` is negative,\n * implements signed->unsigned conversion of modular representatives.\n * Questions of representation are not considered in the specification\n * @[FIPS203, Section 2.4.1, \"The pseudocode is agnostic regarding how an\n * integer modulo 𝑚 is represented in actual implementations\"].}\n *\n * @reference{Embedded in the polynomial compression function in the\n * reference implementation @[REF]. Used as part of signed->unsigned\n * conversion for modular representatives. This happens in `mlk_poly_reduce()`\n * here, and as part of polynomial compression functions in @[REF]. See\n * `mlk_poly_reduce()`. Barrier to reduce the risk of compiler-introduced\n * branches. For `a = MLKEM_Q_HALF` and `b=0`, also embedded in\n * `poly_frommsg()` from the reference implementation, which uses\n * `cmov_int16()` instead.}\n *\n * @param a    First alternative.\n * @param b    Second alternative.\n * @param cond Condition variable.\n *\n * @return @p a if @p cond != 0, else @p b.\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE int16_t mlk_ct_sel_int16(int16_t a, int16_t b, uint16_t cond)\n__contract__(ensures(return_value == (cond ? a : b)))\n{\n  uint16_t au = mlk_cast_int16_to_uint16(a);\n  uint16_t bu = mlk_cast_int16_to_uint16(b);\n  uint16_t res = bu ^ (mlk_ct_cmask_nonzero_u16(cond) & (au ^ bu));\n  return mlk_cast_uint16_to_int16(res);\n}\n\n/**\n * Functionally equivalent to cond ? a : b, but implemented with guards\n * against compiler-introduced branches.\n *\n * @reference{Embedded into `cmov()` in the reference implementation @[REF].\n * Uses a value barrier to get mask from condition value.}\n *\n * @param a    First alternative.\n * @param b    Second alternative.\n * @param cond Condition variable.\n *\n * @return @p a if @p cond != 0, else @p b.\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE uint8_t mlk_ct_sel_uint8(uint8_t a, uint8_t b, uint8_t cond)\n__contract__(ensures(return_value == (cond ? a : b)))\n{\n  return b ^ (mlk_ct_cmask_nonzero_u8(cond) & (a ^ b));\n}\n\n/**\n * Compare two arrays for equality in constant time.\n *\n * @spec{Used to securely compute conditional move in @[FIPS203, Algorithm\n * 18 (ML-KEM.Decaps_Internal, L9-11].}\n *\n * @reference{`cmov()` in the reference implementation @[REF]. We return\n * `uint8_t`, not `int`. We use an additional XOR-accumulator in the\n * comparison loop which prevents early abort if the OR-accumulator is 0xFF.\n * We use a value barrier to convert the OR-accumulator into a mask; the\n * reference implementation uses a shift which the compiler can argue to\n * result in either 0 or 0xFF..FF.}\n *\n * @param[in] a   First byte array.\n * @param[in] b   Second byte array.\n * @param     len Length of the byte arrays, upper-bounded to UINT16_MAX to\n *                control proof complexity only.\n *\n * @retval 0    The byte arrays are equal.\n * @retval 0xFF The byte arrays are not equal.\n */\nstatic MLK_INLINE uint8_t mlk_ct_memcmp(const uint8_t *a, const uint8_t *b,\n                                        const size_t len)\n__contract__(\n  requires(len <= UINT16_MAX)\n  requires(memory_no_alias(a, len))\n  requires(memory_no_alias(b, len))\n  ensures((return_value == 0) || (return_value == 0xFF))\n  ensures((return_value == 0) == forall(i, 0, len, (a[i] == b[i]))))\n{\n  uint8_t r = 0, s = 0;\n  unsigned i;\n\n  for (i = 0; i < len; i++)\n  __loop__(\n    invariant(i <= len)\n    invariant((r == 0) == (forall(k, 0, i, (a[k] == b[k]))))\n    decreases(len - i))\n  {\n    r |= a[i] ^ b[i];\n    /* s is useless, but prevents the loop from being aborted once r=0xff. */\n    s ^= a[i] ^ b[i];\n  }\n\n  /*\n   * - Convert r into a mask; this may not be necessary, but is an additional\n   *   safeguard\n   *   towards leaking information about a and b.\n   * - XOR twice with s, separated by a value barrier, to prevent the compile\n   *   from dropping the s computation in the loop.\n   */\n  return (mlk_value_barrier_u8(mlk_ct_cmask_nonzero_u8(r) ^ s) ^ s);\n}\n\n/**\n * Copy len bytes from x to r if b is zero; don't modify x if b is non-zero.\n * Assumes two's complement representation of negative integers. # PBYTES Theorem Registry V1

## Frozen target

- Campaign: PBYTES
- Public function: `mlk_poly_tobytes`
- Portable body: `mlk_poly_tobytes_c`
- Source commit: `af4c5abdd5958bdc65a03cd5ee86708264f93304`
- Core theorem families: 4
- Core semantic obligations: 19
- Native-backend semantic claim: excluded

## PBYTES-T1 — Exact arithmetic ByteEncode12 refinement

Independent oracle uses arithmetic division and remainder, not the
production shift-and-mask expressions.

1. PBYTES-T1.P1 — exact low byte of the even coefficient.
2. PBYTES-T1.P2 — exact high nibble of the even coefficient.
3. PBYTES-T1.P3 — exact low nibble of the odd coefficient.
4. PBYTES-T1.P4 — exact high byte of the odd coefficient.
5. PBYTES-T1.P5 — exact 24-bit packed-word equality.
6. PBYTES-T1.P6 — complete 384-byte arithmetic-oracle equality.

## PBYTES-T2 — Exact successor and carry-transition partition

Inputs differ by an increment of one at one selected canonical coefficient.
The incremented value must remain below MLKEM_Q.

1. PBYTES-T2.P1 — even coefficient without low-byte carry.
2. PBYTES-T2.P2 — even coefficient with 255-to-256 carry.
3. PBYTES-T2.P3 — odd coefficient without high-nibble carry.
4. PBYTES-T2.P4 — odd coefficient with 15-to-16 nibble-to-byte carry.

## PBYTES-T3 — Exact canonical image and invalid-codeword exclusion

The independent decoder interprets each three-byte block arithmetically as
W = b0 + 256*b1 + 65536*b2, with fields W mod 4096 and W / 4096.
It must not call mlk_poly_frombytes.

1. PBYTES-T3.P1 — every produced even field is below MLKEM_Q.
2. PBYTES-T3.P2 — every produced odd field is below MLKEM_Q.
3. PBYTES-T3.P3 — every canonical 24-bit block is realizable.
4. PBYTES-T3.P4 — a block with either invalid field is not realizable.
5. PBYTES-T3.P5 — full-array image iff all 256 fields are canonical.

## PBYTES-T4 — Arithmetic recoverability and collision freedom

1. PBYTES-T4.P1 — arithmetic recovery of the even coefficient.
2. PBYTES-T4.P2 — arithmetic recovery of the odd coefficient.
3. PBYTES-T4.P3 — block equality iff coefficient-pair equality.
4. PBYTES-T4.P4 — full canonical-polynomial injectivity.

## Count

- T1: 6
- T2: 4
- T3: 5
- T4: 4
- Total: 19

a861211798b7740f7242393891f5d73708526a2115a530ea26c5a54147cd1fdf  /home/girish/THESIS-2026/mlk_poly_tobytes_cleanroom/PBYTES_00D_THEOREM_FREEZE_af4c5abd/registry/PBYTES_SCOPE_AND_NONCLAIMS_V1.md

# PBYTES Scope and Nonclaims V1

## Proof target

The semantic harnesses shall call the public `mlk_poly_tobytes` wrapper in a
portable configuration whose GOTO call graph reaches `mlk_poly_tobytes_c`.

Calling only the file-local portable body and then claiming public-wrapper
correctness is prohibited.

## Permitted assumptions

- Input polynomial is a valid local object.
- Output is a valid 384-byte local object.
- Input and output do not alias.
- Every input coefficient is in `[0, MLKEM_Q)`.
- T2 incremented coefficients remain in `[0, MLKEM_Q)`.
- T3 arbitrary encoded inputs may be constrained only by the explicitly
  tested canonical-field predicate.
- Selected indices are within their recorded ranges.

## Forbidden proof transformations

- No production-source modification in the positive theorem run.
- No replacement of `mlk_poly_tobytes` by a contract.
- No replacement of `mlk_poly_tobytes_c` by a contract.
- No native backend silently selected.
- No call to `mlk_poly_frombytes` inside an independent oracle.
- No reuse of the production shift-and-mask expression as the T1 oracle.
- No assumption of the expected output relation.
- No contradictory or result-shaped assumptions.
- No stubbing of the target function.
- No fixed-point or round-trip theorem presented as a new primary family.
- No generic locality, frame or determinism theorem counted as a new family.

## Mandatory assurance controls

- Exact source and commit binding.
- GOTO call-graph binding.
- Complete unwinding.
- Memory and arithmetic safety.
- Assertion reachability.
- Boundary-case reachability.
- Input-frame preservation.
- Output canaries.
- Complete output overwrite.
- Nonconstant-output witnesses.
- Mutation sensitivity.
- Deterministic evidence and hash freezing.

## Nonclaims

- Native AArch64 or x86-64 semantic correctness.
- Constant-time execution or side-channel resistance.
- `mlk_poly_frombytes` correctness.
- Compression or decompression correctness.
- Complete ML-KEM correctness.
- Out-of-domain behaviour.
- Mathematical or worldwide first-ever novelty.
